transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. I, uh, I guess I'm here because... well, it's a little hard to explain exactly, but I've just been feeling so incredibly off lately. You see, I'm an executive administrative assistant, so my entire life, my whole career really, is built around keeping a perfectly clean calendar. I mean, color-coded, everything scheduled down to the minute, anticipating what my boss needs before he even knows he needs it. It's usually something I take a lot of pride in, something that makes me feel grounded and like myself. 

But lately, well, for a little while now, it’s just... it's all started feeling so incredibly flat. And heavy. Like I'm trying to move through wet concrete just to look at my schedule. And it's not just work, which is the scary part. It's the things outside of work that usually make me feel alive. I usually do these long photography walks on the weekends—I have this camera I love taking down by the river, trying to catch the morning light on the water, framing the perfect shot. It used to bring me so much joy. And I mentor some of the local neighborhood kids, helping them with homework and just, you know, being a positive presence. I've been doing that for years. 

But now? I just... I just stopped initiating any of it. I don't call the kids' parents to set up times, I don't pick up my camera, I look at my pristine calendar and just feel this immense weight. I just sit there. I don't know why the spark is just completely gone, but it really isn't like me to just let everything drop like this, especially the organizing, because usually I'm the one keeping everyone else on track, you know? So I figured I needed to come in and figure out why everything feels so empty.
Have you ever felt this way for a period of two weeks or longer at any point in your life before this current episode?

No, doctor, I really haven't. And I think that's exactly why I'm sitting here talking to you today, because it's just so unprecedented for me. 

I mean, sure, everyone has a bad day here and there, right? Sometimes the office gets incredibly stressful, like if we're preparing for a massive quarterly board meeting and my boss is breathing down my neck, or if a major catering order falls through at the last minute. When things like that happen, I might feel totally drained for a weekend. I might just want to sit on my couch on a Sunday and not look at a single spreadsheet or email. But two whole weeks? Or longer? Never. Absolutely never. 

I've been in my line of work for over twenty years now, and you just don't survive as an executive assistant at this level if you're checking out for weeks at a time. I am the anchor for my team. People rely on me to be the one who never drops the ball. If I had ever felt this heavy, this... disconnected from my calendar, from my photography, from the neighborhood kids... for that long in the past, I would have noticed immediately. My boss certainly would have noticed. My whole filing and scheduling system would have completely collapsed. 

I remember back in, oh, it must have been 2015 or maybe 2016, we had this massive corporate merger, and I was working these grueling seventy-hour weeks. I was physically exhausted, sure, but I never lost my spark, you know? I never lost that underlying drive to organize and color-code and keep things moving. Even when I was dead tired, I still wanted to grab my camera on a Saturday morning. So this feeling right now, this total flatness and emptiness that just drags on and on, day after day, week after week... this is entirely new territory for me. I've never experienced a stretch like this in my entire forty-six years. It's just so completely alien to who I am and how I operate.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your sleep patterns since you began feeling this way?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask about sleep, because that's actually been one of the strangest parts of all this. It's completely thrown off my nighttime routine, and I am very big on routines, as you can probably imagine. Usually, I'm in bed by 10:30 PM sharp, I read for exactly thirty minutes—non-fiction usually, right now I'm reading this fascinating book on the history of urban planning—and then lights out at 11:00 PM. I usually get a solid seven or eight hours, wake up at 6:30 AM, make my coffee, and I'm out the door. 

But lately? It's like my internal clock is just completely broken. Or maybe not broken, but running on some bizarre alternate timezone. There have been these nights, and it's happening more often than I'd like to admit, where I'll get maybe two, sometimes three hours of sleep tops. I'll wake up at, say, 2:15 in the morning. Pitch black outside. The whole house is completely silent. And you would think, given how heavy and flat I've been feeling during the day, that I'd just roll over and go back to sleep, right? Or at least feel exhausted. 

But no, I wake up before dawn and I don't feel tired at all. It's the strangest sensation. It's like a switch flips in the middle of the night. Suddenly, instead of feeling like I'm moving through that wet concrete I mentioned earlier, I'm lying there in the dark and all I can think about is work. I feel completely wide awake, almost wired, and I just have this intense urge to get up and start answering emails. Or I'll think about my boss's travel itinerary for next month and feel this sudden, pressing need to get out of bed, open my laptop, and start updating his appointment lists right then and there. I'll actually sit at my kitchen island at 3:00 AM, in the dark, reorganizing spreadsheets that don't even need to be looked at for another three weeks. It makes no sense, because during normal working hours I can barely bring myself to look at the calendar, but then at three in the morning on two hours of sleep, I'm suddenly ready to tackle the entire quarter's scheduling. It's just so confusing, doctor.

During those times when you are awake at 3:00 AM feeling wired and productive, do you feel an unusually high or intense sense of energy, or perhaps a feeling of being 'on top of the world' that is different from your usual self?

Well, yes, actually, now that you put it that way. It's... it's a very specific kind of feeling. It's not just that I'm awake and not tired, it's like I have these stretches where I feel unusually upbeat, just incredibly dialed in. I'll be sitting there at the kitchen island at three in the morning, and I just feel this absolute certainty that everything is clicking perfectly into place. Like I'm conducting a symphony, you know? Every email, every spreadsheet, it all just makes total sense and I feel like I'm ten steps ahead of my boss, ten steps ahead of everyone else in the building. It’s this fantastic, soaring feeling where I'm just absolutely on top of it all, and it sometimes carries right over into the morning when I get to the office. 

But the strange thing is—and this is what really bothers me because it's so unprofessional—that feeling is incredibly volatile. Because while I'm in that zone, feeling so upbeat and capable, if even one tiny thing disrupts my flow... well, it’s like a completely different switch flips. 

For example, just the other day, I had perfectly orchestrated the entire afternoon schedule for the executive team. Everything was color-coded, everything was set. And then one of the junior marketing directors—nice kid, usually, fresh out of college—sent a message saying he needed to move his 2:00 PM meeting by just fifteen minutes. Fifteen minutes! Normally, I handle rescheduling in my sleep, it's my job. But in that moment, when I was feeling so high and productive? I just snapped. I was so incredibly sharp with him. I mean, my tone was just biting. I practically interrogated the poor guy about his time management skills right there in the open office. 

I walked back to my desk and thought, 'Who was that?' It completely surprised me, because I pride myself on being the calm center of the storm. I am the diplomatic one. But lately, during these wired stretches, I just get so incredibly snappy if anyone touches my perfectly arranged puzzle. It's just so out of character to be that upbeat and on top of the world one minute, and then practically biting someone's head off the next just over a minor calendar adjustment. It really threw me.
Have you ever experienced these periods of feeling 'on top of the world' and wired for a week or longer, or were they ever so intense that you required professional intervention or hospitalization?

Hospitalized? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I mean, I've always managed to keep showing up to the office and keeping the executive suite running, even when I'm feeling that intense buzz. I've never needed to go to a hospital or even see a professional about it before now, because, well, in the corporate world, being incredibly driven and needing barely any sleep is usually something people praise you for, right? They think you're just a real go-getter, a dedicated company man. 

But to answer your question about how long it lasts and if it's been a week or longer... if I really sit and think about it—and I actually keep very meticulous records, I have all my old daily planners color-coded by year on this beautiful mahogany bookshelf in my den, so I can track my own productivity—if I trace it back, these specific stretches... these periods where I'm just so elevated, so incredibly driven, running on practically zero sleep and walking around with just, frankly, way too much confidence... they've actually been recurring for about eleven months now. 

Yes, it would be right around eleven months. I remember the first time it really kicked into high gear was during the prep for last year's Q3 fiscal review. I just thought I was highly motivated because we had a new Vice President of Operations and I wanted to make a stellar impression. I was strutting into boardroom meetings to hand out the morning agendas feeling like I was the CEO myself, just absolutely untouchable. I was completely overstepping my usual boundaries, but I felt so brilliant doing it. 

It’s just this recurring cycle that’s been happening for almost a year. I'll get into one of these stretches and feel totally invincible, buzzing with all that energy for a week or two, and then it settles down, and then a month or two later it comes right back. So, no, I've never been hospitalized or had anyone stage an intervention, but this pattern of getting so wired and overconfident? It's definitely been cycling through my life for about eleven months. It's just that I never really saw it as a problem until this current, awful heavy feeling hit me, because before this, the high energy just made me feel like the most effective assistant on the eastern seaboard.

During those times when you felt invincible and incredibly driven for a week or more, did you ever feel like your energy or behavior was so intense that it caused significant problems in your work performance or social life?

Well, "significant problems" might be putting it a bit strongly, because, as I said, I pride myself on keeping the ship afloat no matter what. My work has stayed intact overall, thank goodness. The executive suite hasn't collapsed. But... well, it’s the nuances, you know? The things that used to be completely automatic for me are suddenly taking effort. 

For instance, I've always had a mind like a steel trap for scheduling. If you asked me what time the CFO's flight lands in Chicago next Tuesday, I wouldn't even need to look at my screen, I'd just know it. But during these stretches, I’ve actually missed some calendar details. Just silly, uncharacteristic errors, like almost booking a car service for 4:00 PM instead of 4:00 AM, or forgetting to factor in the time zone change for a Zoom call with the London office. Because my mind is moving so fast, I just sort of skip over the basics. So I’ve had to start obsessively double-checking tasks that I used to do in my sleep. I'll sit there staring at an itinerary I just made, tracing my finger over the monitor, reading it three or four times because I just don't trust my own brain to have caught everything the first time. It's maddening, frankly, because flawless efficiency is my entire brand at that company. 

And then outside of work... yes, it has affected things there, too, now that I think about it. I'm quite passionate about photography—mostly architectural and street photography, I absolutely love capturing the juxtaposition of old brick buildings against modern glass skyscrapers, and I even have a whole digital editing setup in my den—but I've completely pulled back from my weekend photography outings. I used to go out every single Saturday morning, rain or shine, but I just stopped. 

And I've also stepped away from this mentoring program I'm involved with. I usually mentor a couple of the junior administrative staff, helping them navigate corporate politics and teaching them advanced organizational skills, which is something I take a great deal of pride in. But I've just had to cancel on them lately, or make up excuses about being too busy, because... well, I just don't feel as present or reliable. When I'm buzzing like that, or when my mind is racing a million miles a minute, I can't actually be there for someone else. I might be physically sitting across from a junior assistant at a coffee shop, but mentally I'm ten steps down the road, re-running spreadsheets in my head or obsessing over some grand new filing system. It just didn't feel fair to the people I was supposed to be mentoring, and honestly, I couldn't even focus enough to frame a decent photograph anyway if I tried. So I just sort of quietly withdrew from all of it.

During those times when you felt invincible and incredibly driven, have you ever had an episode that lasted for at least one full week where your energy and behavior were so intense that they significantly interfered with your ability to work or maintain your usual responsibilities?

Well, no, not *significantly* interfered. I mean, I know I just went on about having to double-check my calendar entries and stepping back from my photography—which, by the way, I really do miss, especially right now with the autumn light hitting those pre-war brick facades downtown, it's just a spectacular time of year for shooting—but as far as completely derailing my ability to work for a full week? No, absolutely not. 

I have never, ever let it get to a point where the executives were left fending for themselves. I mean, can you imagine? If I just couldn't maintain my responsibilities for a week, the entire C-suite would be in absolute chaos. They wouldn't know how to log into their own conference calls! I remember one week specifically, back in March, I was in one of those incredibly driven states, just buzzing and wired, and we had the quarterly shareholder meeting coming up. Now, normally, that is a logistical nightmare on a good day. I was running on maybe two hours of sleep a night for six days straight, feeling absolutely invincible, but I didn't drop a single ball. I coordinated the A/V team, the catering—we had this highly specialized gluten-free, vegan menu for the new board member from California, which was a whole separate headache to organize—and I managed all of it flawlessly. 

I was double and triple-checking my spreadsheets, sure, like I mentioned before, because my mind was racing so fast I didn't quite trust my own eyes, but I got it done. The meeting went off without a hitch. So, no, it's never interfered to the point where I couldn't do my job or where I just couldn't function for a week. I always push through. I am the glue that holds that office together, Doctor, so I just don't have the luxury of letting my responsibilities slide, no matter how intense that energy gets or how fast my brain is spinning. I just grip the steering wheel a little tighter and keep driving, if that makes sense.

patient.answer:
Hospitalized? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I mean, I've always managed to keep showing up to the office and keeping the executive suite running, even when I'm feeling that intense buzz. I've never needed to go to a hospital or even see a professional about it before now, because, well, in the corporate world, being incredibly driven and needing barely any sleep is usually something people praise you for, right? They think you're just a real go-getter, a dedicated company man. 

But to answer your question about how long it lasts and if it's been a week or longer... if I really sit and think about it—and I actually keep very meticulous records, I have all my old daily planners color-coded by year on this beautiful mahogany bookshelf in my den, so I can track my own productivity—if I trace it back, these specific stretches... these periods where I'm just so elevated, so incredibly driven, running on practically zero sleep and walking around with just, frankly, way too much confidence... they've actually been recurring for about eleven months now. 

Yes, it would be right around eleven months. I remember the first time it really kicked into high gear was during the prep for last year's Q3 fiscal review. I just thought I was highly motivated because we had a new Vice President of Operations and I wanted to make a stellar impression. I was strutting into boardroom meetings to hand out the morning agendas feeling like I was the CEO myself, just absolutely untouchable. I was completely overstepping my usual boundaries, but I felt so brilliant doing it. 

It’s just this recurring cycle that’s been happening for almost a year. I'll get into one of these stretches and feel totally invincible, buzzing with all that energy for a week or two, and then it settles down, and then a month or two later it comes right back. So, no, I've never been hospitalized or had anyone stage an intervention, but this pattern of getting so wired and overconfident? It's definitely been cycling through my life for about eleven months. It's just that I never really saw it as a problem until this current, awful heavy feeling hit me, because before this, the high energy just made me feel like the most effective assistant on the eastern seaboard.

doctor.question: During those times when you felt invincible and incredibly driven for a week or more, did you ever feel like your energy or behavior was so intense that it caused significant problems in your work performance or social life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My work has stayed intact overall, but I’ve missed calendar details and had to double-check tasks that used to be automatic. I’ve also pulled back from photography outings and mentoring because I don’t feel as present or reliable.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the intense energy and behavior caused significant problems in work performance or social life, which directly assesses functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, "significant problems" might be putting it a bit strongly, because, as I said, I pride myself on keeping the ship afloat no matter what. My work has stayed intact overall, thank goodness. The executive suite hasn't collapsed. But... well, it’s the nuances, you know? The things that used to be completely automatic for me are suddenly taking effort. 

For instance, I've always had a mind like a steel trap for scheduling. If you asked me what time the CFO's flight lands in Chicago next Tuesday, I wouldn't even need to look at my screen, I'd just know it. But during these stretches, I’ve actually missed some calendar details. Just silly, uncharacteristic errors, like almost booking a car service for 4:00 PM instead of 4:00 AM, or forgetting to factor in the time zone change for a Zoom call with the London office. Because my mind is moving so fast, I just sort of skip over the basics. So I’ve had to start obsessively double-checking tasks that I used to do in my sleep. I'll sit there staring at an itinerary I just made, tracing my finger over the monitor, reading it three or four times because I just don't trust my own brain to have caught everything the first time. It's maddening, frankly, because flawless efficiency is my entire brand at that company. 

And then outside of work... yes, it has affected things there, too, now that I think about it. I'm quite passionate about photography—mostly architectural and street photography, I absolutely love capturing the juxtaposition of old brick buildings against modern glass skyscrapers, and I even have a whole digital editing setup in my den—but I've completely pulled back from my weekend photography outings. I used to go out every single Saturday morning, rain or shine, but I just stopped. 

And I've also stepped away from this mentoring program I'm involved with. I usually mentor a couple of the junior administrative staff, helping them navigate corporate politics and teaching them advanced organizational skills, which is something I take a great deal of pride in. But I've just had to cancel on them lately, or make up excuses about being too busy, because... well, I just don't feel as present or reliable. When I'm buzzing like that, or when my mind is racing a million miles a minute, I can't actually be there for someone else. I might be physically sitting across from a junior assistant at a coffee shop, but mentally I'm ten steps down the road, re-running spreadsheets in my head or obsessing over some grand new filing system. It just didn't feel fair to the people I was supposed to be mentoring, and honestly, I couldn't even focus enough to frame a decent photograph anyway if I tried. So I just sort of quietly withdrew from all of it.

doctor.intent: Distinguish between Bipolar I and Bipolar II by determining if the patient has ever experienced a full manic episode lasting at least one week or requiring hospitalization.
doctor.question: During those times when you felt invincible and incredibly driven, have you ever had an episode that lasted for at least one full week where your energy and behavior were so intense that they significantly interfered with your ability to work or maintain your usual responsibilities?

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeating a question about whether the episodes caused significant interference with work or responsibilities (functional impairment), which the patient already answered in the previous turn. There are no other unrevealed symptoms in the profile that specifically address marked impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not *significantly* interfered. I mean, I know I just went on about having to double-check my calendar entries and stepping back from my photography—which, by the way, I really do miss, especially right now with the autumn light hitting those pre-war brick facades downtown, it's just a spectacular time of year for shooting—but as far as completely derailing my ability to work for a full week? No, absolutely not. 

I have never, ever let it get to a point where the executives were left fending for themselves. I mean, can you imagine? If I just couldn't maintain my responsibilities for a week, the entire C-suite would be in absolute chaos. They wouldn't know how to log into their own conference calls! I remember one week specifically, back in March, I was in one of those incredibly driven states, just buzzing and wired, and we had the quarterly shareholder meeting coming up. Now, normally, that is a logistical nightmare on a good day. I was running on maybe two hours of sleep a night for six days straight, feeling absolutely invincible, but I didn't drop a single ball. I coordinated the A/V team, the catering—we had this highly specialized gluten-free, vegan menu for the new board member from California, which was a whole separate headache to organize—and I managed all of it flawlessly. 

I was double and triple-checking my spreadsheets, sure, like I mentioned before, because my mind was racing so fast I didn't quite trust my own eyes, but I got it done. The meeting went off without a hitch. So, no, it's never interfered to the point where I couldn't do my job or where I just couldn't function for a week. I always push through. I am the glue that holds that office together, Doctor, so I just don't have the luxury of letting my responsibilities slide, no matter how intense that energy gets or how fast my brain is spinning. I just grip the steering wheel a little tighter and keep driving, if that makes sense.
